The Joke That Needed Another Line

需要多说一句的玩笑 · 647 词 · 8 段 · 首次出现的目标词加粗

1A town invited two communities to share an evening of stories. Its organizer asked Sara, a fluent translator, to put subtitles under a recording from an older storyteller. The man spoke a local dialect with a soft accent. A short phrase sounded like an insult when translated word for word. An editor wanted to remove it. Sara noticed the storyteller wink as he said it. His listener laughed. The literal meaning did not convey what the two people appeared to understand.

2Sara copied the quotation and marked its punctuation. A dictionary gave the literal sense. It missed what an affectionate voice could do with the phrase. An older translator said it originated as a proverb about a slow horse. It might sound ridiculous to someone who did not know the culture. Between friends it could show warmth. In anger it could be an insult. Fluency meant noticing how a speaker chose to pronounce it and how a listener replied.

3The woman in the recording recalled the missing line. A neighbor had brought food after a storm. The joke was an implicit acknowledgement of his help. His reply made that explicit. He had used the same expression about himself. A cut for length changed the viewpoint and made a friendly exchange look hostile. Sara asked the editor to restore the continuation. A clumsy subtitle was fixable once the missing oral response could be heard.

4Sara chose wording that let both speakers converse naturally. A younger listener wanted to know why the proverb mentioned a horse. Its relation to the present story was unclear. An instructive note explained how travel worked when it originated. The contrast helped viewers see an old notion in a new context. It also showed how cultural diversity could appear in a commonplace exchange. Sara avoided an imitative accent that would characterize a speaker by one feature of his tongue.

5A teacher from a literature class suggested a test on a familiar topic. She read one idiom with careful pronunciation and asked which expression the pupils would choose in their own accent. Some noticed the spelling, others heard the humorous stress on the last word. One student had learned the phrase from a page about grammar. He could interpret it after listening to both speakers. The difference helped Sara decide which explanatory line to keep.

6At rehearsal an impatient presenter rushed the introduction. A deaf visitor saw the subtitles alone and said one caption sounded oddly apologetic. Sara underlined it and asked which word gave that impression. The reader pointed to a formal expression that was prevalent in official notices. They changed it to a friendly reply. The audience could then perceive the warmth without hearing the original tone. Nobody had to guess whether a facial expression was an apology or a wink.

7A leader worried that an English version might betray the story's origin. An influential writer had once made the same mistake. Sara agreed that one interpretation could be subjective. Nevertheless, she showed him the full recording and both translations. The first looked faithful word by word. The second matched the exchange. They chose to preserve both for comparison. A pupil asked whether recitation would help him memorize the line. Sara asked him to say when he might use it, rather than repeat a phrase he could misunderstand.

8The audience laughed after the restored reply. Sara asked the recipient what made the humor work. He said it was not the subject alone. A poetic expression could sound harsh when a listener had missed its purpose. Another translator wanted an authoritative rule that would apply invariably. Sara suggested asking which part of the speaker's attitude mattered, particularly when the translation sounded more formal than mainstream speech. Pupils wrote comments in the English alphabet, then compared their preferences. Amongst them were people who disagreed about the translation but could describe why the last line mattered.

需要多说一句的玩笑

按英文段落顺序对照阅读

1小镇请两个社区的人来分享故事。组织者请熟练的译者萨拉给一段录音加字幕。录音里，年长的讲述者带着轻柔的口音，说的是本地方言。有一句话逐字译出来像在骂人，编辑想把它剪掉。萨拉注意到，那人说话时眨了一下眼，听的人也笑了。两人似乎都明白的那层意思，字面译文没有传达出来。

2萨拉抄下那句话，标上标点。词典能给出字面义，却看不出亲昵的语气会给它添上什么含义。一位资深译者说，这话源自一句讲慢马的谚语。不了解当地文化的人听来可能觉得荒唐，朋友之间说却可以表示亲热，带着怒气说又可能是骂人。熟悉一门语言，也要留意说话的人怎么发音，听的人怎么回应。

3录音里的女士想起了漏掉的那句。暴风雨过后，一位邻居给她送来吃的。她用玩笑含蓄地表达谢意。邻居接下来的回答把这点说清了，因为他也用同一个说法形容自己。剪短录音时，视角跟着变了，原本友好的对话显得有敌意。萨拉请编辑把下半句放回来。只要听得到那句口头回应，生硬的字幕就有办法改。

4萨拉挑了能让两人自然交谈的措辞。一位年轻观众想知道，谚语为什么要提到马。这跟眼前的故事有什么关系，还不太清楚。一条简短的注释介绍了谚语产生的年代，人们是怎么出行的。观众由此看到，同一种老观念可以用在新的语境里，一段家常对话也能体现文化差异。萨拉没有刻意模仿口音，因为那样容易让人只凭说话的一种特点来评判这个人。

5文学课老师建议用大家熟悉的话题试一试。她仔细念出一个习语，问学生用自己的口音表达时会选哪种说法。有的留意了拼写，有的听出了末尾重读带来的幽默。一个学生曾从语法书上学过这个说法，听过两个人的对话后，他才读懂这里的意思。这种差别帮萨拉决定了该留哪一句说明。

6排练时，急性子的主持人匆忙念完了介绍。一位听障观众只看字幕，觉得有一句莫名像在道歉。萨拉在下面划了线，问是哪个词让他这么觉得。对方指出，那是官方通知里常见的一种正式说法。他们换成了朋友间的回答。现在观众就算听不见原声，也能感到亲切，还能分辨人物脸上是歉意，还是眨眼逗趣。

7一位负责人担心英文版会偏离故事的来处。一位颇有影响力的作家就犯过这个错误。萨拉认同，单凭一个人的理解可能有些主观。她放了完整录音，也给他看两种翻译。第一版逐字看来忠实，第二版则贴合两人的对话。他们决定两版都留作对照。一个学生问，反复朗读能不能记住这句话。萨拉请他说出自己可能在什么时候用它，这样才知道背下来的意思有没有弄错。

8观众听到补回的那句后笑了。萨拉问收到这句玩笑的人，为什么它好笑。对方说，光知道题材还不够。没听出说话的目的，一句富有诗意的表达也可能很刺耳。另一位译者想找一条到哪里都适用的权威规则。萨拉建议先问，说话人的哪一层态度最重要，尤其当译文比日常说法更正式时。学生们用英文字母写下评论，再比较各自的偏好。其中有些人不赞同对方的翻译，但都能说明为什么最后那句话重要。
